results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. Creatures phasing back in do not trigger enter-the-battlefield abilities. Phasing in is not a zone change; the permanent never left the battlefield. Rule 702.26d explicitly states that zone-change triggers (which include enters-the-battlefield triggers, as defined in rule 603.6a) don't trigger when a permanent phases in or out. The game treats the phased-out permanent as though it doesn't exist, but it remains on the battlefield the whole time, so no "enters" event occurs when it phases in.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: Yes, deathtouch changes how trample assigns excess damage. Because any nonzero amount of combat damage from a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for trample purposes [702.2c], a creature with both trample and deathtouch only needs to assign 1 damage to each blocking creature to satisfy the lethal-damage requirement. The rest of its damage can then be assigned to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle as excess. This is confirmed by the excess-damage rule: “Any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source dealing that damage to a creature has deathtouch” [120.4a]. The trample rule itself says to check for assigned lethal damage without considering abilities that might change the amount actually dealt [702.19b], but deathtouch directly modifies what counts as lethal during assignment, so it is taken into account. In short: with deathtouch, 1 damage per blocker is lethal, and the rest tramples over.

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes, storm is a triggered ability, and it can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Rule 702.40a defines storm as a triggered ability that functions on the stack. Rule 113.9 states that activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren't spells, so they can't be countered by effects that counter only spells, but they can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Therefore, the storm triggered ability is a legal target for something like Stifle or Disallow, but not for a simple counterspell like Counterspell.

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: No, you cannot. A card with a hybrid mana symbol has all colors of that symbol in its color identity. For example, a card with a {R/G} hybrid symbol has both red and green in its color identity. Commander deck construction requires that every color in a card's color identity be present in your commander's color identity. If your commander's color identity is only one of those colors (say, red only), then the card's green color identity is not in the commander's color identity, so the card is illegal. This is explicitly stated in rule 903.5c, which uses Wort, the Raidmother (color identity red and green) as an example: each card in that deck must be only red, only green, both, or colorless. A card with a {R/G} symbol is both red and green, so it would be allowed in a red-green deck but not in a mono-red deck. The definition of color identity (903.4f) includes all mana symbols in mana cost and rules text, and hybrid symbols are colored mana symbols that are all their component colors (107.4e).

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast or abilities activated or resolved. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held and put onto the stack at the beginning of the upkeep step, before the active player gets priority.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes. Creatures that were declared as attackers (or put onto the battlefield attacking) remain attacking creatures during the end of combat step. According to the definition of an attacking creature, a creature remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. The end of combat step is part of the combat phase, and the combat phase doesn’t end until after the end of combat step ends (rule 511.3). Therefore, during the end of combat step, those creatures are still attacking creatures unless they’ve been removed from combat by some other effect. The end of combat step itself has no turn-based actions that would remove them (rule 511.1).

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Lands are never cast as spells. Instead, you play a land as a special action that doesn't use the stack. This means putting a land card from your hand onto the battlefield during your main phase while the stack is empty and you have priority, and it doesn't count as casting a spell. Even if a card is both a land and another card type (like an artifact land), it can only be played as a land and cannot be cast as a spell. Lands have no mana cost, so they are played without paying any costs.

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: Yes, you can sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves. The evoke ability creates a triggered ability that goes on the stack when the creature enters the battlefield (rule 702.74a). As with any triggered ability, players can respond to it with instants or activated abilities before it resolves (rule 603.3d). If you sacrifice the creature in response (for example, by activating an ability of another permanent), the evoke trigger will still resolve, but it won't be able to sacrifice the creature because it's no longer on the battlefield. You won't have to sacrifice it again.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes, losing all abilities includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are a subset of abilities (rule 702.1). An effect that says an object "loses all abilities" removes every ability it has, including any keyword abilities (rule 113.10b). This is confirmed by rule 603.6b, which explicitly states that an effect reading "All creatures lose all abilities" causes a creature to lose its abilities the moment it enters the battlefield, preventing even enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities (which are often keyworded) from triggering. Ability-removing effects are applied in layer 6 alongside ability-adding effects and keyword counters (rule 613.1f), further showing that keyword abilities are treated as abilities subject to removal.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if your hand is already at your maximum hand size. The maximum hand size (normally seven, or six with a vanguard card's hand modifier of -1) only matters during your cleanup step: at that time, if you have more cards than your maximum, you must discard down to that number [402.2, 514.1, 703.4n]. There is no rule that prevents you from drawing cards when your hand is full. You may draw cards, and then later in the turn you'll discard the excess during cleanup. If an effect says you can't draw cards for some other reason (like a replacement effect or a restriction), that's separate, but the maximum hand size itself does not stop you from drawing.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: A planeswalker with 0 loyalty counters is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. This happens automatically the next time state-based actions are checked, without using the stack and before any player receives priority. Loyalty is defined as the number of loyalty counters on the planeswalker [306.5c], so having 0 counters means its loyalty is 0. The state-based action that moves it to the graveyard is explicitly listed: "If a planeswalker has loyalty 0, it's put into its owner's graveyard" [704.5i, 306.9]. Damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from it [120.3c, 306.8], which can reduce its loyalty to 0 and trigger this action. The rules provided do not address negative loyalty counters; a planeswalker's loyalty cannot be less than 0 because counters are removed one by one, and once it reaches 0, the state-based action applies immediately.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No, non-creature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" is defined in the rules as meaning "is put into a graveyard from the battlefield" and applies only to creatures and planeswalkers. A non-creature artifact that is put into a graveyard from the battlefield is simply moved to the graveyard; it does not "die" for rules purposes.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: You lose the game the next time state-based actions are checked. When you attempt to draw a card from an empty library, no card is actually drawn because there are none to take. Then, before any player receives priority, the game checks state-based actions and sees that you attempted to draw from an empty library, causing you to lose (rules 121.4, 704.5b, 104.3c). This applies whether the draw is mandatory or you choose to draw (you are allowed to choose to draw even if your library is empty, per 121.3 and 121.3a). If an effect replaces the draw (e.g., “If you would draw a card, instead …”), that replacement is applied even though the library is empty (121.6a, 614.11), and you might not lose depending on what the replacement does.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. If no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, the declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped. If any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, there are two combat damage steps instead of one.

As the defending player, you get priority during each of these steps after the active player passes priority. Specifically, at the start of each step (after any turn-based actions and triggered abilities are put on the stack), the active player receives priority first. Once the active player passes, you (the defending player) receive priority. The only exception is during the combat damage step: after combat damage is assigned (a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack), damage is dealt simultaneously, and no player gets priority between assignment and dealing. After damage is dealt and state-based actions are checked, the active player gets priority, then you get priority when they pass.

In a two-player game, the defending player is the nonactive player, so you are the next player in turn order after the active player. In multiplayer games, the defending player may be one opponent chosen by the active player (depending on the variant) or all opponents; priority then passes in turn order among all players, so you may not be the very next player to receive priority after the active player unless you are next in turn order.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Activated mana abilities don't use the stack; they resolve immediately after being activated, so they can't be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Triggered mana abilities similarly resolve immediately without using the stack. This is because mana abilities follow special rules that bypass the stack entirely.

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a cost being paid. Paying a cost is not an event that uses the stack; it is performed as part of a larger action—such as casting a spell, activating an ability, or declaring attackers or blockers—during which no player receives priority. The rules explicitly provide a window to activate mana abilities before costs are paid (see rules 118.2, 601.2g, 508.1i, 509.1e), but once the actual payment begins, it happens immediately and without interruption. No player can cast spells or activate non-mana abilities in response to the payment itself.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are the system Magic uses to determine the order in which continuous effects modify an object's characteristics. You start with the object's printed values (or the values defined by the effect that created it, for a token or copy), then apply all applicable continuous effects in a strict sequence of layers. The layers, in order, are:

- **Layer 1**: Copiable values — copy effects, merging, and "as . . . enters" / "as . . . is turned face up" abilities that set power and toughness [613.1a, 613.2a]. After this layer, the object's characteristics are its copiable values [613.2c].
- **Layer 2**: Control-changing effects (inferred from the Act of Treason example in [613.6]).
- **Layer 3**: Text-changing effects [613.1c].
- **Layer 4**: Type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d].
- **Layer 5**: Color-changing effects [613.1e].
- **Layer 6**: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that say an object can't have an ability [613.1f].
- **Layer 7**: Power- and toughness-changing effects, applied in sublayers:
  - **7a**: Characteristic-defining abilities that define power and/or toughness [613.4a].
  - **7b**: Effects that set power and toughness to a specific value (e.g., "becomes 0/1") [613.5 example].
  - **7c**: Effects that modify power and toughness without setting them (e.g., +1/+1 counters, "gets +4/+4") [613.5 example].

Within each layer or sublayer, effects are normally applied in **timestamp order** — the effect with the earlier timestamp applies first [613.7]. However, if one effect **depends on** another (it's in the same layer/sublayer, applying the other would change the first effect's text, existence, what it applies to, or what it does, and neither or both are from characteristic-defining abilities), the dependency system overrides timestamp order [613.8, 613.8a]. In layers 2–6, characteristic-defining abilities are always applied before other effects [613.3].

An effect that does multiple things (e.g., "gains control and gains haste") is split across the relevant layers — each part applies in its appropriate layer, and once an effect starts applying in one layer, it continues to apply to the same set of objects in later layers even if the source of the effect is removed [613.6]. The entire layer system operates continuously and automatically; any change to an object's characteristics is instantaneous [613.5].

For example, if you control Honor of the Pure ("White creatures you control get +1/+1") and a 2/2 black creature, and an effect turns that creature white (layer 5), it immediately gets +1/+1 (layer 7c) and becomes 3/3. If its color later changes to red (layer 5 again), the bonus stops and it returns to 2/2 [613.5].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that causes a player who controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name to choose one and put the rest into their owners' graveyards. It applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype (rule 205.4d), including planeswalkers, which now have the legendary supertype (rule 306.4). The rule is defined in rule 704.5j: "If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards." This happens automatically whenever state-based actions are checked, which occurs before any player would receive priority (rule 117.5), and it doesn't use the stack (rule 704.1).

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Your creature dies as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked after the damage is marked. That check happens before any player would receive priority, so it occurs immediately after the spell, ability, or combat damage step that dealt the damage finishes resolving. The damage itself doesn't destroy the creature; rather, the game sees that the creature has toughness greater than 0 and damage marked on it greater than or equal to its toughness, and destroys it as a state-based action (rules 704.5g, 120.5).

If the damage is marked during the resolution of a spell or ability (for example, Lightning Bolt dealing 3 damage to a 2/2 creature), state-based actions are not checked until that spell or ability finishes resolving (rule 704.4). So the creature won't die in the middle of the spell; it dies right after the spell resolves, before any player gets priority. Similarly, after combat damage is dealt, state-based actions are checked before the active player gets priority (rule 510.3a, 117.5).

In short, the creature dies at the very next state-based action check following the damage being marked, which is always before any player can cast spells or activate abilities.

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: No, you cannot cast your commander directly from exile. The Commander rules only grant permission to cast a commander from the command zone (rule 903.8). There is no rule that allows casting a commander from exile. However, if your commander is in exile, you may use the state-based action described in rules 704.6d and 903.9a: since the commander was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. Once it's in the command zone, you can cast it from there (paying the commander tax as applicable). This state-based action is optional, so you can leave it in exile if you prefer, but you still won't be able to cast it from exile unless another effect specifically allows casting cards from exile.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
During the cleanup step, the active player first discards down to their maximum hand size if necessary. Then, simultaneously, all damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. Normally, no player receives priority, so no spells can be cast or abilities activated. However, if any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”), those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put onto the stack, and the active player gets priority. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins. If no state-based actions or waiting triggers exist, the step simply ends without any player getting priority.

This sequence is defined by the turn-based actions of the cleanup step [514.1, 514.2] and the exception that allows priority only when state-based actions or triggers demand it [514.3, 514.3a]. The state-based action check follows the normal process [704.3], but if the first check finds nothing, the step ends immediately [704.3, 500.3]. Note that effects that end the turn can also cause triggered abilities to be put on the stack during a cleanup step, potentially leading to an extra cleanup step [724.1f], but the core cleanup step procedure remains as described.

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text:
State-based actions are checked whenever a player would get priority, during the cleanup step, and when an effect ends the combat phase or ends the turn. They are also checked after turn-based actions at the beginning of steps and phases, before triggered abilities are put on the stack and before any player receives priority.

Specifically:
- **Before priority**: Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions, repeating until none are performed, then puts triggered abilities on the stack, and repeats this whole process until no state-based actions occur and no abilities trigger. Only then does the player receive priority [704.3, 117.5]. This includes after spells/abilities resolve, after combat damage (as implied by [510.3a]), and at the start of most steps/phases after turn-based actions [703.3].
- **Cleanup step**: Normally no player gets priority during cleanup, but the game still checks state-based actions. If any are performed (or any triggered abilities are waiting), those state-based actions happen, then triggered abilities go on the stack, and the active player gets priority. After that stack empties, another cleanup step begins [514.3a].
- **Effects that end the combat phase or turn**: When a spell or ability like Mandate of Peace ends the combat phase, or an effect ends the turn, state-based actions are checked as part of that resolution. No player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put on the stack during that check [724.2c, 724.1c].

State-based actions are automatic, don't use the stack, and are not controlled by any player [704.1, 704.2, 405.6f].

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: You can concede the game at any time. Conceding is immediate, doesn't use the stack, and causes you to leave the game and lose. This right cannot be overridden by any card effect (rule 101.1) and applies even if another player controls your turn (rule 723.6). In a Two-Headed Giant game, if you concede, your entire team leaves the game and loses immediately (rule 810.8b).

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is the player whose turn it is. This is stated directly in the rules: "Active Player. The player whose turn it is." and "A player is one of the people in the game. The active player is the player whose turn it is." So, to know who the active player is, you simply identify which player's turn is currently taking place. In a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is, and each player on that team is an active player; however, any ability that refers to "the active player" will have its controller choose one specific active player to apply to.

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The player who cast the spell—the nonactive player—gets priority first. Under rule 117.3c, when a player casts a spell while they have priority, that same player receives priority again immediately afterward. Since only the player with priority can cast a spell (rule 117.1), the nonactive player must have had priority to cast it, and they retain priority after doing so. The active player does not automatically get priority at this point.

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The active player gets priority first after casting a spell. Rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Since the active player must have priority to cast the spell, they regain priority immediately after casting it.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes, you can hold priority to cast more spells after you've cast one or more spells. When you cast a spell, if you had priority before casting it, you receive priority again immediately after the spell becomes cast (rule 601.2i). This means you can cast another spell right away without passing priority to your opponent. You can repeat this as long as you have priority and are legally allowed to cast the spells. Note that this only applies when you had priority before casting the first spell; if you cast a spell during the resolution of another spell or ability (as allowed by an effect like that described in rule 608.2g), you do not receive priority after casting it, so you cannot hold priority in that situation.

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Lore counters are put on Sagas at two distinct times: first, as a replacement effect when the Saga enters the battlefield; second, as a turn-based action during its controller's precombat main phase.

**Entering the battlefield**  
- A Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter (rule 714.3a).  
- A Saga with read ahead enters with a number of lore counters chosen by its controller between 1 and its final chapter number (rules 714.3b, 702.155b). Both are replacement effects (rule 614.1c) that modify how the permanent enters.

**During the precombat main phase**  
- As a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, immediately after a player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities (rules 714.3c, 703.4f, 505.4). This happens every turn for the active player's own Sagas.

These are the only times lore counters are placed on Sagas by the game rules (other effects, like proliferate, may also add counters).

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by an effect that instructs a player to do something later in the game, rather than immediately when the spell or ability that creates it resolves. It contains the words “when,” “whenever,” or “at,” though that word usually does not begin the ability. Delayed triggered abilities are created during the resolution of spells or abilities, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as a result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action. They trigger only once—the next time their trigger event occurs—unless they have a stated duration like “this turn.” If the trigger event occurs more than once simultaneously and the ability lacks a stated duration, the controller chooses which event causes the trigger. The source and controller of a delayed triggered ability depend on how it was created: if created by a spell, the source is that spell and the controller is the player who controlled the spell as it resolved; if created by an activated or triggered ability, the source is the same as that ability’s source and the controller is the player who controlled that ability as it resolved; if created by a static ability generating a replacement effect, the source is the object with that static ability and the controller is that object’s controller at the time the replacement effect was applied; if created by a static ability allowing a player to take an action, the source is the object with that static ability and the controller is that object’s controller at the time the action was taken. A delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects it even if the object changes characteristics, but if that object is no longer in the expected zone when the ability resolves, the ability won’t affect it. If a delayed triggered ability refers to X and X is not defined in its own text, but the spell or ability that created it had a value of X chosen for any of its costs, that same value of X is used. Reflexive triggered abilities (those that trigger “when [a player] [does or doesn’t]” take an action or “when [something happens] this way”) are a special kind of delayed triggered ability that are checked immediately after being created and trigger based on whether the trigger event occurred earlier during the resolution of the spell or ability that created them. An ability that triggers whenever a player earthbends triggers when the delayed triggered ability described in the earthbend keyword action is created.

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instants and sorceries) can have abilities. The most common are **spell abilities**—the instructions on the card that are followed as the spell resolves (rule 113.3a). They can also have **static abilities** that function while the spell is on the stack, such as those that modify how it can be cast or that refer to countering it (rules 604.5, 113.6e). Additionally, an instant or sorcery card may have a triggered ability (e.g., “When you cast this spell…”), but that triggered ability becomes a separate object on the stack, not part of the spell itself. The spell on the stack inherits all characteristics of the card, including any abilities printed on it, so it can certainly have abilities.

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate a mana ability while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second explicitly allows players to activate mana abilities even though it normally prevents casting spells and activating non-mana abilities. Rule 702.61a defines split second as meaning "As long as this spell is on the stack, players can’t cast other spells or activate abilities that aren’t mana abilities," and rule 702.61b further clarifies that players may activate mana abilities and take special actions while a spell with split second is on the stack. Mana abilities themselves don't use the stack and can be activated at times when you normally couldn't activate other abilities, so they are unaffected by the restriction.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first. Divination is countered and does not resolve; it is put into its owner's graveyard.

When all players pass priority in succession, the topmost object on the stack resolves (rule 608.1). Counterspell is on top of the stack targeting Divination, so Counterspell resolves first. Its effect is "Counter target spell." Countering a spell means canceling it, removing it from the stack, and preventing it from resolving (rule 701.6a). Divination is the target, so it is countered, removed from the stack, and placed into its owner's graveyard. Divination never resolves and none of its effects occur.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign at least 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk before you can trample any excess to the defending player. Charging Rhino is a 4/4 with trample, and Vampire Nighthawk is a 2/3 blocker with deathtouch. When assigning combat damage, the attacking creature's controller must assign lethal damage to all blockers before trampling over. Lethal damage is normally equal to the blocker's toughness (3 in this case), taking into account damage already marked and simultaneous damage from other sources, but ignoring abilities that would change the damage actually dealt. The deathtouch ability of the blocker does not affect this calculation because the source dealing the damage—Charging Rhino—does not have deathtouch. Rule 702.2c only makes a nonzero amount of damage lethal when the source dealing that damage has deathtouch. Therefore, Charging Rhino must assign 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk, and the remaining 1 damage can be assigned to the defending player.

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggered ability will resolve **before** the cascaded spell resolves.

When Shardless Agent's cascade ability resolves, you may cast the exiled noncreature spell during that resolution (rule 608.2g). Casting that spell causes Monastery Swiftspear's prowess to trigger immediately (rule 601.2i), but triggered abilities that fire during the resolution of a spell or ability aren't put onto the stack until after that spell or ability finishes resolving (rule 704.4). So the prowess trigger waits until cascade is completely done. At that point, the cascaded spell is already on the stack (it was put there during cascade's resolution), and the prowess trigger is placed on top of it. Because prowess always goes on the stack above the spell that caused it (Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2), it will resolve first, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 before the cascaded spell resolves.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text:
Yes, state-based actions will destroy the Grizzly Bears before your Lightning Bolt resolves.

After you cast Lightning Bolt, the game checks state-based actions before any player gets priority (rule 704.3, 117.5). At that moment, Grizzly Bears has 2 damage marked on it and toughness 2, so it has been dealt lethal damage (rule 704.5g). The state-based action destroys Grizzly Bears immediately, while Lightning Bolt is still on the stack. Lightning Bolt will then be countered on resolution for having no legal target, but the destruction of Grizzly Bears happens before that point.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Both triggers go on the stack at the beginning of your upkeep, before you get priority. You (the active player) put your Phyrexian Arena trigger on the stack first, then your opponent puts their trigger on top. Because the opponent's trigger is on top, it will resolve before your Phyrexian Arena trigger.

This assumes the opponent's trigger actually triggers during your upkeep — for example, if it says "At the beginning of each upkeep" or "At the beginning of each player's upkeep." If the opponent's trigger is worded "At the beginning of your upkeep" (referring to the opponent's own upkeep), it would not trigger at all during your upkeep, and only your Phyrexian Arena trigger would go on the stack.

**When they trigger:** According to rule 500.6, abilities that trigger "at the beginning of" a step or phase trigger when that step or phase begins. So both triggers fire as soon as your upkeep starts.

**How they are ordered:** Rule 503.1a says that before the active player gets priority, all abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put on the stack. Rule 603.3b then governs the order: first, the active player (you) puts each triggered ability you control with a trigger condition that isn't another ability triggering on the stack in any order you choose. Then, the nonactive player (your opponent) does the same. This follows APNAP order (rule 101.4). Since the opponent's trigger is placed on the stack after yours, it ends up on top and resolves first.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
Only the original sorcery card returns to your hand — one card. The copy created by Fork does not return to your hand.

When you cast the sorcery and pay its buyback cost, the buyback ability creates a replacement effect: as the spell resolves, instead of going to the graveyard, it goes to its owner’s hand (rule 702.27a). Fork creates a copy of that spell on the stack. The copy is not a card; it’s a spell-copy with no physical card associated with it (rule 707.10). Because the copy isn’t a card, it can’t be put into a hand. Fork ruling #8 explicitly states: “If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you.” After the copy resolves, it would normally go to the graveyard, but as a copy it ceases to exist instead (rule 704.5e). So only the original card returns to your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. Mimic Vat ruling #0 explicitly covers this situation: if the creature that died was a manifested instant or sorcery card, Mimic Vat may exile that nonpermanent card, but you cannot create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card. When the activated ability resolves, no token is created.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both exiled creatures return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability and its leaves-the-battlefield ability are linked (rule 607.2a). Lithoform Engine's copy of that triggered ability is also linked to the same return ability, as stated in Lithoform Engine's fourth ruling. That ruling explicitly says: "If Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability is copied and two creatures are exiled, they both return when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield." The return ability's wording "the exiled card" is interpreted as referring to all cards exiled by the linked exile abilities, so both creatures are returned.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text:
No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield.

Banishing Light's ability exiles a permanent "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield." Phasing out does not cause a permanent to leave the battlefield—it is merely treated as though it doesn't exist, but it never changes zones (rule 702.26d). Because Banishing Light hasn't left the battlefield, the condition for the exile to end hasn't been met. Teferi's Protection ruling #21 explicitly confirms that one-shot effects waiting for a permanent to leave the battlefield (like Banishing Light's) won't happen when that permanent phases out. The exiled creature remains in exile, and will only return if Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield later (e.g., by being destroyed or exiled while phased in).

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes, your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell while it's on the stack. Protection from instants only applies while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield; as a spell on the stack, it does not have that protection (see Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2). Counterspell can legally target and counter Emrakul, the Promised End.

Even if Emrakul, the Promised End is countered, you still control the targeted opponent's next turn. The ability "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn..." triggers when you finish casting the spell, not when it resolves. Once the spell is cast, the triggered ability goes on the stack above it (rule 601.2i). Counterspell can be cast in response to that trigger, countering Emrakul, the Promised End, but the triggered ability remains on the stack and will resolve independently, giving you control of that opponent's next turn.

This answer applies regardless of the number of players; the interaction works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text: The provided rules do not define the mana value of a modal double-faced card while it is in exile. Cascade requires exiling cards until you hit a nonland card whose mana value is less than the cascade spell's mana value, but without a rule specifying whether Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor has mana value 2 (its front face) or some other value in exile, it is impossible to determine if it is a legal cascade hit. The ruling [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16] allows you to cast a modal double-faced card with any face that fits the criteria of an effect that lets you cast it from among a group of cards, but that ruling does not address the mana value used for the cascade hit condition itself. Therefore, the question cannot be answered with the given rules context.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You control **one** of that opponent's turns (their next turn). You **do** get a second Emrakul, the Promised End — a token copy. Copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell **does not** give you another control-a-turn trigger.

Here's why:

1. **Copying the cast trigger** — Lithoform Engine's first ability copies the triggered ability "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn." The copy is put on the stack and you may choose new targets. Assuming you target the same opponent, both the copy and the original trigger will resolve. Each creates a continuous effect that would control that opponent's next turn and then give them an extra turn. However, multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other; the last one created is the one that works. The original trigger resolves after the copy, so its effect is the last one created and will control the opponent's next turn. The copy's effect is overwritten for the "next turn" control, but it still creates an extra turn after that turn (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14). So you control exactly one of that opponent's turns (the next one), and that opponent will take two extra turns afterward (neither of which you control). If you had chosen a different opponent for the copy, you would control one turn of each of those opponents.

2. **Copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell** — Lithoform Engine's third ability copies the permanent spell. The copy is put on the stack and is not cast (rule 707.10). When it resolves, it becomes a token with the characteristics of Emrakul, the Promised End (rule 111.13). So you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token.

3. **No extra cast trigger** — The copy of the spell was not cast, so its "When you cast this spell" ability does not trigger (Lithoform Engine ruling #6; rule 707.10). You do not get another control-a-turn trigger from the token copy.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Yes, you get two tokens.

When you activate Mimic Vat's ability, it goes on the stack. You then copy that ability with Lithoform Engine. The copy is put on the stack and, according to rule 707.10, it copies all characteristics and decisions of the original ability. The copy's source is the same as the original's source—Mimic Vat (rule 707.10 and Lithoform Engine ruling #0). When the copy resolves, it looks at the card exiled with Mimic Vat (the imprinted creature) and creates a token that's a copy of that card, with haste and the exile clause. The original ability then resolves and does the same. Since the exiled card exists, rule 111.12 does not prevent token creation. You end up with two token copies of the exiled creature.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, the total cost is {3} (three generic mana) and you create zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. To get value, you should choose X=2 or greater. With X=2, you pay {1}{G}{G} and create two tokens; this is the smallest X that avoids Trinisphere's cost-setting effect and gives you tokens efficiently.

Reasoning: The total cost of a spell is determined in this order: start with the mana cost ({X}{G}{G}), add cost increases, subtract cost reductions, then apply Trinisphere's effect if the mana component is less than three mana (rule 601.2f, Trinisphere ruling #0). Your cost reduction of {1} is generic mana, so it reduces only the generic mana component of the cost (rule 118.7a).

- For X=0, the mana cost is {G}{G} (no generic component). The {1} reduction does nothing, leaving the cost at {G}{G} (two mana). Trinisphere sees a cost of less than three mana and sets the total cost to {3}. You pay {3} and get X=0 tokens.
- For X=1, the mana cost is {1}{G}{G}. The reduction lowers the generic part by {1}, making the cost {G}{G} (two mana). Trinisphere again sets it to {3}. You pay {3} and get one token.
- For X=2, the mana cost is {2}{G}{G}. After the {1} reduction, the cost is {1}{G}{G} (three mana). Trinisphere does not apply because the cost is not less than three mana. You pay {1}{G}{G} and get two tokens.
- For larger X, the cost after reduction is {X-1}{G}{G}, which is always at least three mana, so Trinisphere never applies. The rate of tokens per mana improves as X increases (e.g., X=3 costs {2}{G}{G} for three tokens).

Thus, X=2 is the minimum choice that yields tokens without Trinisphere interference, and any higher X gives even better value if you have the mana.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text: Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide in your graveyard with Animate Dead because Grist, the Hunger Tide's static ability makes it a 1/1 Insect creature card while in the graveyard, so it's a legal target for Animate Dead's "enchant creature card in a graveyard." When Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability resolves, it returns Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control and tries to attach Animate Dead to it. However, on the battlefield Grist, the Hunger Tide is no longer a creature (it's just a planeswalker), so Animate Dead can't legally enchant it. As a state-based action, Animate Dead is put into its owner's graveyard. This causes Animate Dead's delayed triggered ability ("When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it") to trigger. When that trigger resolves, you must sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide. The net result is that Grist, the Hunger Tide enters the battlefield briefly, then is sacrificed and returns to the graveyard.
citations: Grist, the Hunger Tide static ability

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters. No, Doubling Season does not double them.

Skullbriar's ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." The command zone is not a hand or library, so when you move Skullbriar there (assuming the Commander replacement effect that allows this, which is not included in the provided rules), the counters stay on it. When you later cast Skullbriar, it moves from the command zone to the stack and then to the battlefield — again, none of those zones are a hand or library, so the counters remain. This overrides the general rule that counters cease to exist when an object changes zones (rule 122.2).

Doubling Season's second ability replaces an effect that would "put one or more counters on a permanent you control." However, the counters that stay on Skullbriar through zone changes are not being "put" on it by any effect; they simply persist. As stated in Skullbriar's ruling #2, "The counters that remain on Skullbriar as it changes zones aren't 'placed' on Skullbriar. Effects like Doubling Season's ... won't affect those counters." Therefore, Doubling Season does not double the four +1/+1 counters when Skullbriar enters the battlefield.
citations: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ability text

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text:
No, you do not lose the game during that extra turn. However, the delayed triggered ability from Final Fortune (“At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game”) does not simply vanish — it will trigger at the beginning of the next turn’s end step instead, so you will lose the game at that time unless you can prevent it.

When you activate Sundial of the Infinite before the end step, the turn ends immediately and the end step is skipped entirely [724.1d]. Because the end step is skipped, “at the beginning of the end step” triggered abilities don’t trigger during that turn [724.1e]. Sundial of the Infinite’s own ruling clarifies that such abilities will trigger at the beginning of the end step of the next turn [Sundial of the Infinite ruling #1]. Therefore, Final Fortune’s lose-the-game trigger is postponed to the next turn’s end step, and you will lose then unless you take further action to stop it.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, after the Clone spell resolves. Your opponent cannot respond to that choice because it's not a spell or ability on the stack; it's a replacement effect that modifies how Clone enters. The opponent can respond to the Clone spell while it's on the stack, but they won't know what you'll choose until Clone is already entering.

Clone's ability is a replacement effect that says "You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield." This choice is made as part of the event of Clone entering the battlefield, not during the casting process. Rule 707.6 explains that when an object enters as a copy, its controller makes any "as [this] enters the battlefield" choices at that time. Clone's ability doesn't target (Clone ruling #0), so you don't announce a target while casting. Once Clone resolves, it enters, and you immediately choose a creature to copy. No player gets priority during this process, so the opponent can't respond to the choice itself. They could have responded to the Clone spell earlier, but they wouldn't know what you'd pick.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text: You get three lands. The original Flooded Strand ability and the two copies created by Gogo, Master of Mimicry are separate objects on the stack. Each resolves independently, instructing you to search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle. Because each resolution includes a shuffle before the next ability resolves, the searches are not combined under rule 701.23h; you perform three distinct searches, each finding one land. The copies don't require any additional costs (life payment or sacrifice) because they are copies of the ability, not new activations.
